The Equal Rights Amendment, passed by Congress in March 1972, was ratified by 30 states in its first year, but momentum slowed; Indiana became the 35th and final state to ratify before the original deadline, on 18 January 1977. No further states ratified between then and the 22 March 1979 deadline, leaving the total three short of the 38 (three-fourths of the states) needed for adoption. 35 states. Congress sent the ERA to the states on 22 March 1972 with a seven-year ratification deadline of 22 March 1979. By that date 35 of the required 38 states (three-fourths of the 50 states) had ratified it — leaving it three short. (Complicating matters, five of those states — Nebraska, Tennessee, Idaho, Kentucky and South Dakota — had passed measures purporting to rescind their ratifications, though the validity of such rescissions is legally disputed.) Congress subsequently extended the deadline to 30 June 1982, but no additional states ratified during the extension; Nevada (2017), Illinois (2018) and Virginia (2020) ratified long afterward, raising the total to 38, though the legal effect of those late ratifications remains contested.

Four. The five conventionally named Great Lakes are Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario. Because Lake Michigan and Lake Huron are joined at the Straits of Mackinac — a wide (about 5 miles/8 km), deep channel with no appreciable drop in elevation — they share the same surface level (about 577 ft / 176 m) and behave hydrologically as a single lake, often called 'Lake Michigan–Huron.' Treating that combined basin as one lake leaves four: Superior, Michigan–Huron, Erie, and Ontario. Incidentally, Lake Michigan–Huron so defined is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area (roughly 45,000 sq mi / 117,000 km²), exceeding Lake Superior.

Four. The Great Lakes are conventionally counted as five — Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario — but Lake Michigan and Lake Huron are hydrologically a single lake (often called "Lake Michigan–Huron"), joined at the Straits of Mackinac, which are about 5 miles wide and 120 feet deep with free exchange of water in both directions and the same surface elevation (~577 ft / 176 m). Counting them as one body gives four Great Lakes: Superior, Michigan–Huron, Erie, and Ontario. On that basis, Michigan–Huron is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area (about 45,300 sq mi / 117,300 km²), surpassing Lake Superior.

Notes: (1) Tipped employees may be paid a cash wage as low as $2.13/hour, provided tips bring total earnings to at least $7.25/hour (the employer must make up any shortfall). Strictly speaking, none — because on 1 January 2006 the IAU had no formal definition of a "planet" and had never adopted a resolution enumerating the planets. By long-standing convention, however, the IAU (like the rest of the astronomical community) treated the Solar System as having nine planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and Pluto. The matter was unsettled at that moment: the object 2003 UB313 (later named Eris), announced in July 2005 and larger than Pluto, had prompted claims of a "tenth planet," and an IAU working group was deliberating on a definition. That definition came only with IAU Resolution B5 at the General Assembly in Prague on 24 August 2006, which set the count at eight planets and reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet."

Two caveats worth noting: (1) the IAU had no formal, written definition of 'planet' at that date, so the count of nine was inherited convention rather than a codified ruling; and (2) the recently announced 2003 UB313 (later named Eris), discovered in 2005 and touted by some as a 'tenth planet', had not been granted planetary status by the IAU. The formal definition — which created the 'dwarf planet' category, reclassified Pluto and Eris into it, and left eight planets — was adopted only later that year, by IAU Resolution 5A at the General Assembly in Prague on 24 August 2006.

A typical adult human skeleton has 206 bones. (Infants are born with roughly 270–300 separate bones and cartilage elements, many of which fuse during growth — e.g., the sacrum, coccyx, and the ilium/ischium/pubis of the hip bone — leaving the standard adult count of 206.) This figure is divided into the axial skeleton (80 bones: skull, ossicles, hyoid, vertebral column, ribs, and sternum) and the appendicular skeleton (126 bones: limbs plus the shoulder and pelvic girdles). Note that the exact number can vary slightly between individuals due to variations such as extra (sesamoid) bones, cervical ribs, or extra vertebrae.

Eight. The IAU's 2006 definition (Resolution B5, adopted at the General Assembly in Prague on 24 August 2006) requires that a planet be a celestial body that (a) is in orbit around the Sun, (b) has sufficient mass for its self-gravity to overcome rigid body forces so that it assumes a hydrostatic equilibrium (nearly round) shape, and (c) has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. The eight bodies meeting all three criteria are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Pluto fails the third criterion and was reclassified as a "dwarf planet" (along with Ceres, Eris, and later Haumea and Makemake).
